"title": "Characteristics of EGRET Blazars in the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS)",
"authors": "G. B. Taylor, S. E. Healey, J. F. Helmboldt, S. Tremblay, C. D. Fassnacht, R. C. Walker, L. O. Sjouwerman, T. J. Pearson, A. C. S. Readhead, L. Weintraub, N. Gehrels, R. W. Romani, P. F. Michelson, R. D. Blandford, and G. Cotter",
"field_subfield": "Astrophysics: Active Galactic Nuclei / Blazars",
"type_of_paper": "Observational survey analysis paper",
"executive_summary": "This paper examines the radio properties of blazars detected by the EGRET instrument aboard the Compton Gamma-Ray Observatory (CGRO), using data from the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS). VIPS is a large, uniform VLBI survey of flat-spectrum radio sources in the Northern Cap region of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), with a flux limit roughly an order of magnitude below other samples such as MOJAVE. The authors intersect the EGRET catalog with the CRATES radio survey to identify 173 candidate EGRET sources, of which 31 fall within the VIPS region and are uniformly imaged down to 85 mJy at 8 GHz. The study finds that gamma-ray flux density does not directly correlate with radio flux density at lower flux levels, but that EGRET-detected blazars tend to have higher brightness temperatures, greater core fractions, and possibly larger jet opening angles, along with weak correlations with jet length and polarization. These trends are interpreted as evidence for systematically larger Doppler factors in gamma-ray-loud blazars, consistent with higher apparent velocities measured at radio frequencies above 10 GHz. The findings have implications for source selection strategies for the GLAST (now Fermi) gamma-ray telescope, suggesting that selecting sources with large core fractions, high central brightness temperatures, and large opening angles may be advantageous. The paper acknowledges limitations due to small sample sizes and incomplete redshift distributions, which constrain the statistical power of the analysis. The results support models in which gamma-rays are produced in jets oriented at small angles to the line of sight, and they anticipate that improved statistics from GLAST will confirm tighter beaming angles for gamma-rays.",

summary.title: Characteristics of EGRET Blazars in the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS)
summary.authors: G. B. Taylor, S. E. Healey, J. F. Helmboldt, S. Tremblay, C. D. Fassnacht, R. C. Walker, L. O. Sjouwerman, T. J. Pearson, A. C. S. Readhead, L. Weintraub, N. Gehrels, R. W. Romani, P. F. Michelson, R. D. Blandford, and G. Cotter
summary.executive_summary: This paper examines the radio properties of blazars detected by the EGRET instrument aboard the Compton Gamma-Ray Observatory (CGRO), using data from the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS). VIPS is a large, uniform VLBI survey of flat-spectrum radio sources in the Northern Cap region of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), with a flux limit roughly an order of magnitude below other samples such as MOJAVE. The authors intersect the EGRET catalog with the CRATES radio survey to identify 173 candidate EGRET sources, of which 31 fall within the VIPS region and are uniformly imaged down to 85 mJy at 8 GHz. The study finds that gamma-ray flux density does not directly correlate with radio flux density at lower flux levels, but that EGRET-detected blazars tend to have higher brightness temperatures, greater core fractions, and possibly larger jet opening angles, along with weak correlations with jet length and polarization. These trends are interpreted as evidence for systematically larger Doppler factors in gamma-ray-loud blazars, consistent with higher apparent velocities measured at radio frequencies above 10 GHz. The findings have implications for source selection strategies for the GLAST (now Fermi) gamma-ray telescope, suggesting that selecting sources with large core fractions, high central brightness temperatures, and large opening angles may be advantageous. The paper acknowledges limitations due to small sample sizes and incomplete redshift distributions, which constrain the statistical power of the analysis. The results support models in which gamma-rays are produced in jets oriented at small angles to the line of sight, and they anticipate that improved statistics from GLAST will confirm tighter beaming angles for gamma-rays.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper examines the radio properties of blazars detected by the EGRET instrument aboard the Compton Gamma-Ray Observatory (CGRO), using data from the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS). VIPS is a large, uniform VLBI survey of flat-spectrum radio sources in the Northern Cap region of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), with a flux limit roughly an order of magnitude below other samples such as MOJAVE. The authors intersect the EGRET catalog with the CRATES radio survey to identify 173 candidate EGRET sources, of which 31 fall within the VIPS region and are uniformly imaged down to 85 mJy at 8 GHz. The study finds that gamma-ray flux density does not directly correlate with radio flux density at lower flux levels, but that EGRET-detected blazars tend to have higher brightness temperatures, greater core fractions, and possibly larger jet opening angles, along with weak correlations with jet length and polarization. These trends are interpreted as evidence for systematically larger Doppler factors in gamma-ray-loud blazars, consistent with higher apparent velocities measured at radio frequencies above 10 GHz. The findings have implications for source selection strategies for the GLAST (now Fermi) gamma-ray telescope, suggesting that selecting sources with large core fractions, high central brightness temperatures, and large opening angles may be advantageous. The paper acknowledges limitations due to small sample sizes and incomplete redshift distributions, which constrain the statistical power of the analysis. The results support models in which gamma-rays are produced in jets oriented at small angles to the line of sight, and they anticipate that improved statistics from GLAST will confirm tighter beaming angles for gamma-rays.

Research Context
At high galactic latitudes, most sources seen by EGRET are identified with blazars. Blazars exhibit flat radio spectra, rapid variability, and superluminal motion. Prior studies reported conflicting radio properties for EGRET blazars. Existing samples used to study EGRET blazars have high flux limits. Prior work suggested EGRET blazars have more strongly polarized jets. The relationship between gamma-ray and radio flaring remains unclear. Two classes of gamma-ray blazars have been proposed. Existing samples are limited by their flux limits.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question concerns correlations in parsec-scale jet properties of EGRET blazars. The study hypothesizes that gamma-ray selection biases toward higher Doppler factors. Higher Doppler factors should manifest as higher core fractions and brightness temperatures. The study predicts larger jet opening angles for EGRET blazars. The study predicts a lack of direct correlation between gamma-ray and radio flux. The study predicts faster apparent motions consistent with higher Doppler factors. The predicted outcome is that gamma-ray selection tightens beaming.

Methodological Details
The survey is the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS). VIPS covers 1127 flat-spectrum sources stronger than 85 mJy. VIPS was carried out between January and August 2006. VIPS includes 5 GHz full polarization images of 958 sources. VIPS includes 147 total intensity images from the CJF survey. Over 99% of VIPS sources were successfully imaged. The EGRET catalog was compared to the CRATES survey. The comparison yielded 173 candidate EGRET sources at |b| > 10 degrees. The study focuses on 31 EGRET candidate blazars in the VIPS region. The VIPS region covers approximately 5700 square degrees. The flux limit is 85 mJy at 8 GHz. The Figure of Merit uses 8.4 GHz flux, spectral index, X-ray flux, and position. Sources are classified as likely if FoM > 1. Sources are classified as plausible if 0.25 < FoM < 1.0. The sample includes 12 likely and 19 plausible candidates. The minimum beam FWHM used was 3 mas. The restoring beam FWHM was 3 mas.

Procedures And Architectures
The classification uses the scheme of Helmboldt et al. (2007a). Brightness temperatures come from automatic modelfits to source components. Sources with two or fewer components were fitted to visibility data directly. Only image plane modelfitting was carried out in Helmboldt et al. (2007a). The minimum observable size was calculated using equation (2) from Kovalev et al. (2005). The core size minimum is approximately 10% of all VIPS sources. Observed brightness temperatures are computed without rest-frame correction. The opening half-angle is measured using a specific formula. The opening angle is only measured for sources with more than 2 total components. Jet bending was calculated by fitting a parabola to centroids. The K-S test is used to compare distributions. Monte-Carlo simulations were used to test opening angle significance.

Key Results
Radio flux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray flux density. EGRET blazars have higher brightness temperatures than average. The K-S test probability for core brightness temperature is 4%. The jet component brightness temperature distributions look fairly similar. The K-S test for jet component brightness temperature is 11%. The source classes are 8 PS, 3 SJET, and 14 LJET. Applying the same classification to MOJAVE sources adds 5 LJET and 1 SJET. Polarization is detected from all 6 MOJAVE sources and 9 of 25 VIPS sources. The total polarization is 48 ± 12%. The VIPS overall polarization average is 36 ± 4%. The LJET polarization average is 41 ± 4%. The core fraction K-S test probability is 4%. The EGRET sources appear biased toward more core-dominated systems. The jet opening angle K-S test probability is 30%. Three sources have jet opening half-angles exceeding the VIPS median. The VIPS median opening half-angle is 18.9 degrees. Six sources have opening angles larger than 20 degrees. The jet length K-S test probability is 34%. The number of PS sources is 8 ± 3. The number of SJET sources is 7 ± 3. The number of LJET sources is 13 ± 4. The number of CSO sources is 3 ± 2. The polarization excess is marginally significant.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The trends support models with jets oriented at small angles to the line of sight. Higher Doppler factors explain the observed trends. The trends explain higher core fractions, brightness temperatures, and polarization. The trends explain faster motions. The large opening angles indicate a sight-line close to the beaming cone. The unbiased comparison supports the higher Doppler factor hypothesis. The statistics are poor due to only 4 sources with enough jet components. The evidence for long jets is of marginal significance. The a priori prediction for fixed jet length and modest velocity is shorter jets. Longer jets might indicate intrinsically greater surface brightness. The redshift distribution for VIPS is incomplete. The gamma-ray flux density is not simply related to the radio flux density. The results anticipate confirmation of tighter beaming angles with GLAST.

Contradictions And Limitations
The relationship between radio and gamma-ray flaring is unclear. The polarization statistics are limited by small sample sizes. The mix of frequencies complicates polarization analysis. No k-corrections have been applied to the core fraction. The opening angle statistics are based on very small samples. Only 4 sources have enough jet components for unbiased analysis. The jet bending results are inconclusive. The jet length comparison shows no appreciable difference. The selection bias investigation is hampered by incomplete redshift distribution. The source J17246+6055 has no known redshift or spectroscopic classification. The morphology of J09576+5522 is ambiguous. The diffuse emission in some blazars complicates the opening angle calculation.

Claims
EGRET-detected blazars have higher Doppler factors than the radio-selected population at large. Higher core fractions are observed in EGRET blazars. Higher brightness temperatures are observed in EGRET blazars. Higher polarization is observed in EGRET blazars. The unbiased comparison supports the higher Doppler factor hypothesis. The trends explain the observed properties. The unbiased comparison has poor statistics. The jet length evidence is of marginal significance. The selection bias investigation is hampered by incomplete redshift distribution. The results support models with jets oriented at small angles to the line of sight. The results anticipate confirmation of tighter beaming angles with GLAST. The results suggest new source selection strategies for GLAST.
The gamma-ray flux density is not simply related to the radio flux density. At lower flux levels, radio flux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray flux density. The gamma-ray flux density is not simply related to the radio flux-density. The relationship between radio and gamma-ray flaring is unclear. Selecting the brightest radio sources may not maximize coincidence with strong gamma-ray emission. New source selection strategies are needed for GLAST. Contemporaneous ground-based monitoring is important.

Data And Code Availability
The VIPS images are available online. The VIPS images are available at the University of New Mexico. The full radio/gamma-ray properties of the sample will be discussed in Healey et al. 2007b. The core flux density for the EGRET blazars can be found in Table 3. The core sizes, core TB, brightest jet component TB, δPA, and jet opening half angle are in Table 3.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The K-S test is used to compare distributions. The Monte-Carlo simulations test the opening angle significance. The number of PS sources is 8 ± 3. The number of SJET sources is 7 ± 3. The number of LJET sources is 13 ± 4. The number of CSO sources is 3 ± 2. The polarization excess is marginally significant.

Ethical Considerations
The authors thank an anonymous referee for constructive suggestions. The National Radio Astronomy Observatory is a facility of the National Science Foundation.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 plots gamma-ray mean and peak fluxes against 8.4 GHz radio flux density. Fig. 2 shows the 5 GHz VIPS images or 15 GHz MOJAVE images for all 12 sources. Figs. 3 and 4 show the images for 19 sources identified as plausible counterparts. Fig. 5 plots the distribution of core-to-jet ratio for EGRET candidates. Fig. 6 shows the brightness temperature distributions. Fig. 7 shows the jet opening angles and bending. Table 1 summarizes the results. Table 2 shows the source classification. Table 3 provides the core sizes, core TB, brightest jet component TB, δPA, and jet opening half angle.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of higher Doppler factors in EGRET blazars. 2. The strongest evidence is the higher core fractions and brightness temperatures. 3. The future path is to confirm tighter beaming angles with GLAST.
